paragraphs: Rabbi Vastini, in Resh Lakish’s time: end of Bava Metzia 117a, Vastini said in Resh Lakish’s name. Rashi explains: Resh Lakish’s student. The Arukh, entry kar, writes on Bava Metzia 117: “The lower resident supplies the ceiling, the upper the plaster layer.” It explains: reeds or boards with which one roofs a house are called tikrah, ceiling; the clay placed on them and smoothed with a roller is called maazivah. A different explanation is in entry maazev; see Arukh there. Mussaf HaArukh writes concerning this: “The first explanation is difficult according to Arukh’s reading in maazev: ‘What is maazivah? Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says reeds, senaim and clay; Resh Lakish says boards.’ Thus what the Arukh writes here fits neither opinion. But our reading fits: ‘What is tikrah? Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says reeds and senaim ….’ The other explanation fits Arukh’s reading, which is correct: the Gemara does not explain familiar words, only unfamiliar ones. Tikrah is familiar, from korah, beam; maazivah is uncommon, so it asks, ‘What is maazivah?’ Having reached this, let us say Arukh correctly read ‘reeds, senaim and clay’—vetina—not our reading ‘Vastina said in Resh Lakish’s name,’ which Rashi explains as a sage’s name. We do not find this name in the Talmud, and it is unfitting to designate a Torah scholar by Stini, an expression of Satan. Even if we leave the reading ‘What is tikrah? Rabbi Yose bar Chanina says reeds and senaim,’ vetina fits, because clay binds the reeds and senaim and is part of the ceiling; other clay is spread over the ceiling and called maazivah. Ohalot, chapter Adam VeKelim, explicitly proves maazivah is above the beams; see there.” End of quotation. The author of Mussaf HaArukh adds by subtracting; he conceived trouble and bore falsehood, as though Rashi calls Vastini a sage’s name when this name is absent from the Talmud. Rashi is true and his Torah true: Jerusalem Talmud, end of Bava Metzia, on that matter has Rabbi Yusta in Resh Lakish’s name: “The lower resident supplies the ceiling and boards, and the upper the maazivah.” In Jerusalem Talmud, Yesh Nochalin,halakhah 6, and beginning of Ketubbot chapter 9, Rabbi Yustini had a case before the sages and they held him liable. He stood before Resh Lakish, who told him, “Go down into your property.” Thus Yustini was Resh Lakish’s student; Babylonian Talmud too should read “Rabbi Yustini said in Resh Lakish’s name.” Or the Jerusalem Talmud customarily omits or adds a letter. Yuchasin too lists Vastini here and under yod lists Yustini, Resh Lakish’s student—end of quotation—but did not notice they are one. Yusta or Yustini is frequent in the Jerusalem Talmud (see above, letter yod).
